newsitem.title: BELARUS: Lukashenko bars access to old Belarus parliament.
newsitem.headline: Lukashenko bars access to old Belarus parliament.

text.p: President Alexander Lukashenko's police blocked access to the old Belarussian parliament on Thursday, removing the biggest obstacle to his new constitutional order in the former Soviet republic.
Several dozen deputies who had held out against Lukashenko following his victory in a referendum on Sunday found themselves barred from entering the debating chamber.
Police allowed them in to the building only to empty their desks. Angry deputies blamed Russia, which signalled its backing for Lukashenko.

Deputy Viktor Gonchar, who was sacked as head of the electoral commission by Lukashenko before the referendum, said: "Belarus has received a lesson in democracy Russian-style. Moscow has betrayed the idea of parliamentarism and has received as partner a totalitarian republic."

Russia made clear on Thursday it recognised Lukashenko's new constitution as legitimate. Interfax news agency quoted an anonymous Kremlin spokesman as saying there were "no grounds" for considering the referendum as unconstitutional.
"The police are only letting us in to collect our things," liberal faction leader Stanislav Bogdankevich told Reuters.
"This marks the setting up of a junta through the falsification of the referendum results."

The move effectively completed what critics of the hardline 42-year-old president say has been a creeping bloodless coup since Sunday's vote, in which more than 70 percent of all voters backed his draft of a new constitution.

For three days Belarus had two parliaments but the odds were clearly stacked on the side of the majority who abandoned the old chamber to sit in the new "House of Representatives" loyal to Lukashenko.
On Wednesday deputies backing the president voted unanimously to abolish the old parliament under Lukashenko's approving gaze.

"The opposition will not leave. We will wait for the Belarussian people to wake up," Bogdankevich said. On Wednesday opponents of the president and political parties set up a committee to defend the old 1994 constitution.

Lukashenko is to sign the new constitution approved by the referendum at a ceremony on Thursday evening at 1700 GMT to which foreign ambassadors have been invited. It will automatically extend his term in office by two years and give him wider powers over all other institutions.

Members of the rump parliament saw the writing on the wall on Wednesday when their official phone lines were cut off and there were calls from Lukashenko loyalists for immediate repairs and redecoration in the old chamber.

When they arrived around nine a.m. on Thursday they found the building sealed off by a cordon of police. Deputies including speaker Semyon Sharetsky found more police blocking access to the "Oval Hall" debating chamber.

Deputy Anatoly Lebedko said he and the others still considered their Supreme Soviet the only legitimate parliament. He added: "We will never recognise the new constitution which was adopted by fraud."

Viktor Khomych, president of the Chernobyl committee, said Lukashenko had made it clear that he and other rebel deputies who voted last week to impeach the president would be barred from all state employment. "He will always persecute us."
Belarus's constitutional court frequently clashed with Lukashenko before the referendum but has adopted a low profile since the vote and shown no sign of challenging the president.

Western countries have been mildly critical of Lukashenko but none have withdrawn their ambassadors from Minsk or issued more than mild protests. They too are expected eventually to follow the Russian lead and treat the new parliament as legitimate.
